title: Herbal preparations for children
subtitle: A foundations reading on adapting adult herbal preparations for children, dose, preparation type, and safety principles
excerpt: Children are not small adults in their pharmacological response to herbs. This reading covers the practical principles for adapting adult preparations for children over 1 year: dose scaling by weight (Young's rule and the simpler fraction method), which preparations to avoid entirely, which herbs are safe at appropriate paediatric doses, and the specific safety lines that apply to children that do not apply to adults.
sourceNotes: Original Homemade editorial. Dose-scaling references: Young's rule (historical pharmacological standard); Mills S. & Bone K., Principles and Practice of Phytotherapy (2000), paediatric dosing chapter; EMA Paediatric guideline on paediatric investigation plans, herbal considerations.

glossaryTerms.definition: A traditional paediatric dose calculation formula: child dose = (child's age in years ÷ (child's age + 12)) × adult dose. It gives a conservative starting point for children over 2 years. For children under 2, consult a qualified herbalist, avoid therapeutic doses of most herbs in this age group.

A herbal extract prepared in glycerin rather than alcohol, an alcohol-free alternative to a tincture, suitable for children and anyone avoiding alcohol. Glycerites have a shorter shelf life (1 year vs 2 years for tinctures), extract a narrower range of constituents, and are intensely sweet.

content.text: Children's physiology differs from adults in three ways that matter for herbal preparations. First, their liver enzyme systems are immature, especially under 2 years. Second, their skin absorbs topical preparations more readily. Third, their lower body weight means the dose per kilogram is much higher than the adult volume suggests. Adult preparations need dose adjustment, a change of preparation type, or exclusion entirely for children.
Preparations to avoid entirely in children
Alcohol-based herbal extracts at adult doses: the alcohol content is a real burden for a child's liver. Either use a
instead, or dilute the adult extract dose to a small fraction in plenty of water.

Steam inhalations with concentrated aromatic oils (eucalyptus, thyme, peppermint, camphor): young children's airways are sensitive and there is a risk of throat spasm. This type of inhalation is not suitable for children under 5. Plain steam with no herbs added is safe for under-5s.
Mugwort, yarrow at medicinal dose, and pennyroyal: do not use in children.
Honey in any form for babies under 12 months: risk of infant botulism. This includes herbal preparations sweetened with honey. Use glycerin or maple syrup to sweeten children's preparations instead.

The simplest practical approach is the fraction method. An adult dose is designed for a 70 kg adult. Calculate the child's fraction: a 14 kg child receives 14/70 = 1/5 of the adult dose. A 35 kg child (average 10-year-old) receives 35/70 = 1/2 the adult dose.
gives a more conservative age-based estimate. A 6-year-old: 6 ÷ (6+12) = 6/18 = 1/3 of the adult dose. A 10-year-old: 10/22 = just under half.

Start at the lower end of these estimates. Children are more variable than adults in their herb response, and many children benefit from a dose significantly below the calculated fraction, especially for sedative herbs.
Safe herbs for children, a working shortlist

These herbs have a long tradition of safe use in children at age-appropriate doses. Chamomile, elderflower, and lemon balm: use as an infusion. Thyme infusion: half the adult dose for under-10s. Ginger infusion in small amounts. Fennel infusion for infant colic: dilute well and use very small amounts. Take extra care with babies under 6 months. Calendula external preparations are fine at any age for skin and wound care. Lavender: external use only (bath or compress). Do not give lavender orally to under-5s.

For children under 2, for chronic conditions, or for anything beyond simple acute symptoms: this guidance gives a framework but is not a substitute for consulting a qualified herbalist with paediatric experience. Children can change quickly. Some conditions that seem mild, such as breathing problems in under-5s, need prompt medical care rather than herbal management.
